# Volume 1 — CHAPTER XXX. The Regent’s Class Is Organized

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Placing her knitting upon her lap, THIRZA reclined in her seat. A vague notion crossed her mind that she ought to arrange to get her spectacles replaced on her upcoming visit to town, as her tired eyes had been wearying with great frequency recently.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0000 }

Grey Shutters was enveloped in the complete dusk of November as night approached, leaving the leaping crimson fire inside the stove as the kitchen's sole illumination.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0001 }

Nell sat cross-legged upon the rug before the fireplace, staring toward that radiant light in which the warmth of a hundred past summers emanated from the burning maple logs. Though she had been engrossed in a book, it had fallen onto the floor, leaving her to daydream with a gentle smile gracing her open lips. From the vapor and colors of her active imagination, sparkling castles in Spain were taking form; marvelous, captivating exploits were befalling her in the clouds—escapades that invariably ended in success and failed to entangle her in troubles such as those she encountered in reality.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0002 }

Thirza gazed upon her with a gentleness that would only ever be permitted to show within that gentle blend of shadow and hearth-light. Never could Thirza master the art of a love that manifested readily through transparent expressions and spoken words. Yet, because it was so reserved, her affection for this slender, gray-eyed girl had grown all the more profound and powerful. In truth, she feared that her love might cause her to be excessively lenient. A troubling sensation nagged at her that devoting one’s heart to a mortal being as deeply as she had devoted hers to Nell was somewhat wicked, and she possibly engaged in a kind of subtle atonement for this by exhibiting greater strictness and fault-finding than she would have if the girl meant less to her. Undoubtedly, Nell was completely unaware of the depth of Thirza's love for her. On occasion, it occurred to her with a sense of longing that Thirza proved exceedingly difficult to satisfy and was noticeably devoid of empathy and comprehension. Nevertheless, she invariably halted that train of thought with self-rebuke, recalling everything she owed to Thirza.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0003 }

Thirza broke the silence by stating, “Nell, while you and Isolde were away earlier today, Miss Thorne came to visit.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0004 }

With a sudden jolt and an audible breath, Nell returned from her alterative reality.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0005 }

“Was she? Oh, I am deeply regretful that I was absent. Thirza, why did you not call for me? Isolde and I had merely crossed over into the Whispering Wood. The woods are delightful currently. Every little wood object—the ferns, the satin leaves, and the crackerberries—has fallen asleep, exactly as though a person had tucked them under a leafy blanket until spring. My belief is that a small gray fairy wearing a rainbow scarf tiptoed past during the previous moonlit night and performed it. However, Isolde refused to discuss that very much. Isolde has continuously remembered the scolding from her mother regarding imagining ghosts inside the Whispering Wood. That produced a most harmful impact on the imagination of Isolde. It blighted it. Mrs. Sowerby states that Myrtle Bell is a blighted individual. Upon my asking Opal Pettigrew why Myrtle was blighted, Opal replied that she assumed it occurred because her young man had abandoned her. Opal Pettigrew considers nothing except young men, and her condition worsens as she grows older. Young men are fine enough in their proper place, but pulling them into every single thing is improper, is it not? Isolde and I are giving serious thought to pledging to one another that we shall never wed, but instead remain pleasant old maids and reside together eternally. Isolde has not entirely decided, however, since she considers that perhaps marrying a wild, dashing, evil young man to reform him would be nobler. You know, Isolde and I discuss serious topics frequently now. We sense that our age is so much greater than previously that discussing childish affairs is inappropriate. Thirza, reaching nearly fourteen is such a grave matter. Last Wednesday, Miss Thorne brought all of us girls who have reached our teens down to the brook and conversed with us regarding it. She stated that we could not exercise too much care concerning the habits we established and the ideals we gained during our teens, since our characters would be developed and the basis established for our entire upcoming life once we reached twenty. Furthermore, she mentioned that should the foundation be unstable, building anything truly valuable upon it would be impossible. Isolde and I discussed the subject while returning home from school. Thirza, we experienced extreme solemnity. Consequently, we determined that we would attempt to be exceedingly cautious, establish respectable habits, acquire all possible knowledge, and act as sensibly as we could, in order that our characters would be correctly developed when we turned twenty. Contemplating being twenty is completely terrifying, Thirza. It has such an alarmingly old and mature sound. But what brought Miss Thorne here this afternoon?”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0006 }

“Nell, that is the very thing I wish to inform you of, provided you will allow me an opportunity to speak. You were the subject of her conversation.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0007 }

“With respect to myself?” Nell appeared somewhat frightened. Following that, she grew red in the face and cried out:
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0008 }

“Ah, I am aware of what she mentioned. It was my intention to inform you, Thirza, I truly meant to, but it slipped my mind. Yesterday afternoon during school, Miss Thorne discovered me reading Ben Hur when I ought to have been learning my Canadian history. The book was lent to me by Odette Pullen. My reading of it began during the lunch hour, and the chariot race had just been reached when classes resumed. I was desperate to learn the result—even though I felt certain that Ben Hur was bound to win, as it would lack poetical justice otherwise—which led me to lay the history book open upon the top of my desk and wedge Ben Hur underneath it against my knee. To an observer, I appeared to be engaged in studying Canadian history, you see, whereas I was actually delighting in Ben Hur the entire time. I became so absorbed in the story that Miss Thorne’s approach down the aisle went completely unnoticed by me, until I suddenly glanced upward and saw her standing right there looking down at me with such a reproachful expression. I am unable to describe the deep shame I experienced, Thirza, particularly upon hearing Flossie Tulk giggle. Although Miss Thorne confiscated Ben Hur, she uttered not a single word at that moment. She detained me inside during recess and conversed with me. She explained that I had committed a grave fault in two ways. Firstly, I was misusing time that should have been dedicated to my schoolwork; and secondly, I was tricking my teacher by attempting to give the impression of reading a history book when it was actually a novel. Up to that exact moment, Thirza, I had failed to see that my actions were dishonest. It came as a shock. Tears flowed bitterly from my eyes, and I begged Miss Thorne for her forgiveness, promising never to repeat such a misdeed; I even volunteered to perform penance by refraining from taking even a single glance at Ben Hur for an entire week, refusing even to discover the outcome of the chariot race. Miss Thorne, however, stated that such a measure would not be demanded, and she pardoned me without hesitation. Because of that, I feel it was not particularly gracious of her to come here to talk to you regarding the matter after everything.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0009 }

“Miss Thorne didn't ever bring up any such matter with me, Nell, and you are simply being troubled by your own guilty conscience. Bringing storybooks to school is something you ought not to be doing. As it is, you read an excessive number of novels. Back when I was a girl, looking at a novel was something I wasn't even permitted to do.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0010 }

“Oh, how can you label Ben Hur as a novel when it is actually so religious?” Nell objected. “Naturally, it is slightly too thrilling to count as suitable Sunday reading, so I limit it to weekdays. Furthermore, I refrain from reading any book currently unless Miss Thorne or Mrs. Wace deems it an appropriate book for a girl of thirteen and three-quarters. Miss Thorne extracted that promise from me. One day, she caught me reading a book named, The Lurid Mystery of the Haunted Hall. Opal Pettigrew had lent it to me, and, oh, Thirza, its charm and creepiness were incredible. My veinous blood was simply curdled by it. However, Miss Thorne declared it to be an extremely foolish, unhealthy book, requesting that I cease reading it and any similar ones. I did not object to promising that I would avoid similar books, yet returning that volume without learning its ending was pure agony. Nevertheless, my devotion to Miss Thorne endured the trial, and I surrendered it. Thirza, the things you can accomplish when you are genuinely eager to satisfy someone are truly amazing.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0011 }

“Well, I suppose I will kindle the light and start working,” Thirza remarked. “It is clear to me that listening to Miss Thorne’s message is not what you desire. Nothing appeals to you more than the noise of your own voice.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0012 }

“Oh, truly, Thirza, I am eager to listen to it,” Nell exclaimed apologetically. “Not a single word more will escape my lips—not even one. It is clear to me that I chatter excessively, but I am honestly attempting to conquer the habit, and even if my speech is far too plentiful, still, were you merely aware of the numerous thoughts I desire to voice but hold back, you would afford me a little merit for my restraint. Do go ahead and inform me, Thirza.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0013 }

“So, Miss Thorne wishes to form a group with her proficient pupils who intend to prepare for Regent’s entrance exam. Her plan is to provide them with additional instruction for one hour following the school day. Furthermore, she visited Obed and me to inquire whether we wished for you to be included in it. What is your own opinion on this, Nell? Do you desire to attend Regent’s and qualify as a teacher?”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0014 }

“Oh, Thirza!” Nell sat up on her knees and pressed her hands together. “It’s been my life's dream—at least for these past six months, from the moment Opal and Odette started discussing preparing for the Entrance. However, I kept quiet regarding it, as I assumed it would be completely hopeless. Being a teacher would be wonderful to me. But isn't the cost going to be terribly high? Mr. Pullen claims he spent one hundred and fifty dollars for Sukey to finish, and Sukey was no fool at geometry.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0015 }

“I think that aspect of the situation requires no anxiety on your part. At the time Obed and I took you in to raise, we made up our minds to do right by you and provide a proper schooling for you. My opinion is that a girl ought to be equipped to support herself regardless of whether she will ever need to. As long as Obed and I remain here, Grey Shutters will always be a home for you, yet no one can tell what the future holds in this unpredictable life, so being ready for anything is wise. Therefore, you are free to enter the Regent’s class if you wish, Nell.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0016 }

“Oh, Thirza, I appreciate it.” Wrapping her arms around Thirza’s waist, Nell gazed upward into her face with great sincerity. “I am so thankful to both you and Obed. Also, I will apply myself as diligently as possible and try my utmost to make you proud. Just be aware that geometry won't be my strong suit, though I believe I can keep up in all other subjects through tough effort.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0017 }

“I suppose you will manage fine. Your brightness and diligence were noted by Miss Thorne.” The exact remarks Miss Thorne had made regarding Nell were something Thirza would not have disclosed for anything, as doing so might encourage conceit. “Overworking yourself with your studies is an extreme you do not need to hasten toward. Haste is unnecessary. A year and a half will pass before you are prepared to attempt the Entrance. Miss Thorne remarks, however, that starting early to gain a firm foundation is advisable.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0018 }

“My studies will hold greater fascination for me from this moment on,” Nell uttered happily, “since my life now possesses a goal. Mr. Wace asserts that a purpose in life ought to be held by everyone and followed with devotion. However, he mentions that its worthiness must be confirmed by us beforehand. Wanting to become an educator in the mold of Miss Thorne would be considered a worthy purpose by me, wouldn't it be by you, Thirza? That occupation seems exceedingly grand to me.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0019 }

The Regent’s class was formed when the time came. Hugh Carrow, Nell Harcourt, Opal Pettigrew, Odette Pullen, Flossie Tulk, Wilfred Mott, and Elias Purdy MacKinnon entered it. Isolde Pembroke was not among them, because her parents had no plans to send her to Regent’s. To Nell, this felt like an absolute disaster. Not since the evening when Posy Fay suffered from the croup had she and Isolde been apart in any endeavor. On the night that the Regent’s class stayed behind in school for the first time for extra instruction, Nell watched Isolde depart gradually alongside the rest of the students, heading home by herself along the Aspen Path and Primrose Dell; it took every bit of Nell's self-control to stay in her desk and stop herself from running frantically after her friend. A knot formed in her throat, and she quickly hid behind the cover of her raised Latin grammar to conceal the moisture in her eyes. Nell would not have let Hugh Carrow or Flossie Tulk witness those tears for anything in the world.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0020 }

“Oh, Thirza, I truly believed I was experiencing the bitterness of death, just like Mr. Wace mentioned during last Sunday's sermon, as I watched Isolde depart by herself,” she remarked sorrowfully later that evening. “It struck me how marvelous it might have been had Isolde likewise been planning to study for the Entrance. Yet perfection is unattainable in this flawed world, to quote Mrs. Sowerby. Mrs. Sowerby may not always offer comfort, but one cannot deny she utters numerous accurate statements. Furthermore, my impression is that the Regent’s class will prove thoroughly captivating. Odette and Opal merely intend to train as teachers. That represents the peak of what they aspire to achieve. Opal mentions she plans to instruct for merely two years following her qualification, after which she aims to wed. Odette states she means to dedicate her entire existence to pedagogy and refuse marriage forever and ever, since teaching yields an earned income, whereas a spouse provides no compensation and complains should you request a portion of the revenue from butter and eggs. I suspect Odette talks based on sad personal knowledge, seeing as Mrs. Sowerby claims her father is an absolute old eccentric, plus stingier than second skimmings. Flossie Tulk remarks she attends college simply to gain an education, given that gaining a livelihood will not be required of her; she remarks that naturally the situation varies for charity-dependent orphans—those individuals must exert themselves. Elias Purdy aims to become a minister. Mrs. Sowerby claims that carrying such a name leaves him no alternative choice. I trust I am not being sinful, Thirza, yet the notion of Elias Purdy serving as a minister genuinely amuses me. He represents such a comical-looking youth, possessing that massive chubby face, along with his tiny blue eyes, and ears that flare out like flaps. Still, maybe his appearance will become more scholarly as he matures. Wilfred Mott states his intention to enter politics to serve as a member of Parliament, whereas Mrs. Sowerby asserts he cannot triumph in that field, owing to the fact that every Mott is an honest person, and exclusively rogues achieve political success these days.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0021 }

“What is Hugh Carrow going to be?” Thirza asked, noticing that Nell opened her Cæsar.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0022 }

“I do not know what the life ambition of Hugh Carrow is—assuming he possesses one,” Nell remarked contemptuously.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0023 }

A clear competition now existed between Hugh and Nell. While the contention had formerly been somewhat one-sided, it was now indisputable that Hugh possessed the same resolve to achieve the top rank in class as Nell did. He proved to be an adversary deserving of her strength. The remaining students in the class quietly recognized the pair's supremacy, and it never occurred to them to attempt to rival the two.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0024 }

Ever since that afternoon beside the water when she had declined to hear his entreaty for pardon, Hugh, except for the previously mentioned firm competition, had shown not the slightest acknowledgment that Nell Harcourt existed. He conversed and joked with the remaining maidens, traded volumes and riddles with them, debated studies and schemes, and occasionally accompanied one or another of them back from religious service or the Debating Club. Yet he entirely disregarded Nell Harcourt, and Nell discovered that being disregarded is far from agreeable. It availed her nothing to assure herself with a flip of her hair that it mattered not to her. Far within her erratic, female young spirit, she was aware that it truly mattered, and that were she granted a second opportunity at the Lake of Glassy Waters, her reply would be altogether altered. Quite suddenly, as it appeared, and to her hidden distress, she realized that the former ill will she had harbored toward him had vanished—vanished precisely when its supportive strength was most required. She strove to no purpose as she summoned back each event and feeling of that unforgettable event, trying to experience the former comforting wrath. That afternoon beside the water had seen its final brief flare. Nell came to understand that she had granted pardon and put it out of mind unawares. Nevertheless, the time had passed.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0025 }

And at minimum, no one—not Hugh, nor anyone else, and not even Isolde—was ever to guess the extent of her regret or how intensely she desired that she had avoided being so arrogant and nasty! She made up her mind to “shroud her feelings in deepest oblivion,” and it can be disclosed right now that she accomplished this, with such efficacy that Hugh, who perhaps was not entirely as unconcerned as he appeared, was unable to take solace in any thought that Nell was affected by his payback disdain. His sole miserable solace lay in the fact that she shut down Wilfred Mott, ruthlessly, unceasingly, and without justification.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0026 }

Apart from that, the winter elapsed through a cycle of enjoyable responsibilities and learning. To Nell, the days glided past such as golden beads strung upon the year's necklace. She felt joyful, enthusiastic, and engaged; lessons needed to be mastered and distinction to be gained; charming books required reading; fresh compositions had to be rehearsed for the Sunday-school choir; enjoyable Saturday afternoons were spent at the manse alongside Mrs. Wace; and subsequently, nearly prior to Nell's realization of it, spring returned once more to Grey Shutters and the entire world blossomed again.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0027 }

Academic work lost a little of its appeal at that point; the Regent’s class, kept inside at school as the remaining students dispersed into verdant paths, foliage-draped woods, and grassy field trails, gazed yearningly through the windowpanes and realized that Latin verbs and French assignments had unexpectedly forfeited the interest and enthusiasm they had carried during the chilly winter period. Even Nell and Hugh slowed down and became unconcerned. Educator and pupils were equally relieved when the session concluded and the joyful holiday time spread out brightly ahead of them.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0028 }

“However, your efforts have been commendable over the course of this past year,” Miss Thorne remarked to them during the final evening, “and a fine, cheerful holiday is well earned. Enjoy the outdoors as much as possible and gather a solid supply of wellness, vigor, and drive to sustain you throughout the coming year. Remember, it will be the ultimate test—that final year prior to the Entrance.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0029 }

“Will you return the following year, Miss Thorne?” Flossie Tulk inquired.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0030 }

Flossie Tulk was never hesitant about asking questions, and on this occasion her classmates were thankful for her boldness. Though every single one of them desired an answer, not a student would have ventured to put the query to Miss Thorne, because disturbing rumors had been circulating across the school for a while suggesting that Miss Thorne would not return the following year, having received a job offer in her home district's grade school which she intended to take. In breathless anxiety, the Regent’s class waited to hear her response.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0031 }

“Indeed, I believe I shall,” Miss Thorne remarked. “I considered accepting a position at a different school, yet my decision is to return to Brierley. Honestly, my interest in my students here has developed to such an extent that departing proved impossible. Therefore, I will remain and guide you to the end.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0032 }

“Hurrah!” said Elias Purdy. Never in the past had Elias Purdy been so overwhelmed by his emotions, and for seven days he turned red with embarrassment whenever he remembered it.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0033 }

“Oh, I’m so glad,” said Nell, with eyes that shone. “Dear Thorne, it would be utterly terrible if you failed to return. I do not think I could muster the spirit to continue my studies whatsoever if a different instructor came to this place.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0034 }

Upon arriving at her house that evening, Nell piled every one of her textbooks inside a vintage chest located in the attic, turned the lock, and tossed the key inside the blanket box.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0035 }

“I will not so much as glance at a textbook during the break,” she remarked to Thirza. “Throughout the entire term I have worked as intensely as I humanly could, and I have scrutinized that geometry to the point where I can recite every proposition in book one from memory, even if the lettering is altered. I simply feel weary of all rational things, so I intend to allow my imagination free rein for the season. Oh, there is no reason to be frightened, Thirza. I will keep its freedom within sensible bounds. However, I desire to enjoy a truly splendid, merry time this summer, because perhaps it is the final summer that I will remain a young girl. Mrs. Sowerby claims that should I continue growing taller throughout the coming year just as I did this one, longer skirts will become necessary for me. She remarks that I am becoming nothing but legs and eyes. Once those longer skirts are worn, I will feel compelled to behave accordingly and maintain great dignity. At that point, I fear it will not even be acceptable to hold a belief in fairies; therefore, I plan to trust in them with my entire heart during these months. My feeling is that our holiday will be extremely lively. Shortly, Opal Pettigrew will hold a birthday celebration, while the upcoming month brings both the Sunday-school picnic and the missionary concert. Furthermore, Mr. Pembroke promised that on some night he will escort Isolde and me to the Pale Sands Hotel for a meal. You are aware, I suppose, that they serve dinner there at night. Last summer, Odette Pullen went over on one occasion, and she claims that beholding the electric lights, the floral arrangements, and every woman guest wearing such exquisite gowns was a brilliant spectacle. Odette states that it served as her initial look at high society, an experience she will remember until the day she dies.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0036 }

The following afternoon, Mrs. Sowerby arrived to discover the reason Thirza was absent from Thursday’s Aid meeting. People were aware that a problem existed at Grey Shutters whenever Thirza failed to attend the Aid meeting.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0037 }

“Thirza clarified, “Obed had a bad spell with his heart Thursday, and leaving him didn't feel right to me. Oh, yes, now he's all right again, but those spells come on him more frequently than they used to, so I'm worried for him. He has to be cautious and steer clear of excitement, according to the doctor. Excitement isn't something Obed goes around seeking out anyway, nor did he ever, making that simple enough, yet he is also forbidden from doing any really strenuous labor, and telling Obed to refrain from working is just like telling him to stop breathing. Agatha, come take off your coat and hat. Won't you remain for tea?”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0038 }

“Since you insist so strongly, it could be that I ought to remain after all,” stated Mrs. Agatha, although she possessed no plan whatsoever to act otherwise.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0039 }

As Mrs. Agatha and Thirza were sitting at ease in the parlor, tea was prepared by Nell alongside hot biscuits whose lightness and whiteness were sufficient to challenge the disapproval of even Mrs. Agatha.
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0040 }

“Nell has certainly grown into a truly clever girl, I have to confess,” conceded Mrs. Agatha, while Thirza walked alongside her to the lane's terminus when the sun was setting. “You must find her to be a tremendous assistance.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0041 }

“Indeed she is,” remarked Thirza, “and nowadays she is truly dependable and composed. Previously, I worried that she would not outgrow her foolish habits, yet she managed to, and at present I would gladly rely on her for anything.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0042 }

“When I first arrived three years back, I never imagined she would end up so fine,” Mrs. Agatha remarked. “Goodness gracious, will that outburst of hers ever leave my memory! Upon returning to my house that evening, I told Thomas, ‘Remember what I say, Thomas, Thirza Abernethy will regret the action she has chosen.’ However, I was wrong, and I am genuinely pleased about it. Thirza, I do not belong to that sort of folk who are incapable of admitting when they were in the wrong. Indeed, praise be, that was never my manner. My assessment of Nell was indeed an error, yet it is hardly surprising, given that a stranger, more surprising little rascal of a youth never existed on this earth, that is a fact. Applying the standard methods used for different youngsters could not figure her out. The way she has grown better over these three years, particularly regarding her appearance, is nothing less than marvelous. She has turned into a truly attractive young lady, even if I personally do not care much for that fair, large-eyed look. My preference goes to greater vigor and complexion, such as Isolde Pembroke possesses or Opal Pettigrew. The appearance of Opal Pettigrew is truly striking. Even so—I cannot explain the reason, but whenever Nell stands beside those two, despite being nowhere near as good-looking, she causes them to appear somewhat ordinary and exaggerated—rather like those white June lilies she names narcissus placed next to the large, crimson peonies, that is a fact.”
{: #nw-v01-c30-p0043 }
